title: Curve Lab — Build an EC Arithmetic Library

questions.question: In short-Weierstrass EC arithmetic code, what is the “point at infinity” (𝒪) used for?
options: It is the identity element of the elliptic-curve group
It is a special generator point chosen to maximize security
It is the unique point where y = 0 on every curve
It is the point you get by taking modular inverses of x and y
questions.explanation: 𝒪 is the group identity: P + 𝒪 = P and P + (−P) = 𝒪. Implementations usually represent it with a sentinel (e.g., None or Z=0).

questions.question: In SEC1 compressed point encoding, what information does the first byte (0x02 or 0x03) carry?
options: The parity (least-significant bit) of y so y can be recovered from x
The full y-coordinate XORed with x to save space
The curve id so the parser can select p, a, and b
A checksum proving the point lies on the curve
questions.explanation: Compressed encodings store x and one bit of y (parity). Decompression computes y via a modular square root and then selects the root matching the parity bit.

questions.question: Why does a short-Weierstrass implementation check that 4a^3 + 27b^2 ≠ 0 (mod p)?
options: It ensures the curve is non-singular, so the group law behaves correctly
It ensures the curve has exactly p points, so the group order is prime
It ensures x has a square root for every value in F_p
It ensures point addition never needs a modular inverse
questions.explanation: A zero discriminant means the curve is singular (has a cusp/self-intersection), and the usual EC group law formulas stop defining a proper group.

questions.question: When decoding a compressed point, why can decompression fail even if x is a valid field element?
options: Because x may produce a non-residue RHS, so no y exists with y^2 = RHS (mod p)
Because the parity bit always flips y into a different curve
Because modular inverses do not exist in prime fields for odd p
Because compressed encodings require the curve order n to be prime
questions.explanation: Given x, you compute RHS = x^3 + ax + b. If RHS is not a quadratic residue mod p, there is no y satisfying the curve equation, so decoding must reject.

questions.question: What is the main performance reason to use Jacobian (projective) coordinates for scalar multiplication?
options: They avoid modular inversions inside the add/double loop, postponing inversion to the end
They make the curve automatically non-singular even if the discriminant is zero
They guarantee constant-time execution in any programming language runtime
They remove the need to validate points during decoding
questions.explanation: Affine addition needs an inverse for the slope. Jacobian formulas replace inversions with multiplications and only invert once when converting back to affine.

questions.question: Why is “is the point on the curve?” sometimes not enough as a public-key validation rule?
options: Some curves have cofactors > 1, so an on-curve point can lie in a small subgroup unless you check membership or clear the cofactor
On-curve checks are always wrong because points never satisfy the curve equation in F_p
On-curve checks are slower than scalar multiplication, so you should skip them
If the curve is non-singular, then every on-curve point automatically has prime order
questions.explanation: On-curve only proves the point satisfies the equation, not that it is in the intended subgroup. For cofactor>1 groups you need subgroup checks (n·P=𝒪) or cofactor clearing.

questions.question: Which textbook attack becomes easier if a protocol multiplies an untrusted point by a secret scalar without validation?
options: Invalid-curve / small-subgroup style attacks that can leak information about the secret scalar
Meet-in-the-middle attacks on modular inversion that recover p directly
Chosen-prefix attacks that forge SEC1 encodings without knowing x or y
Collision attacks on the discriminant that force 4a^3 + 27b^2 to be zero
questions.explanation: If you accept attacker-chosen points (including points on other curves or small subgroups), scalar multiplication with a secret can leak bits or reduce secrets modulo small factors.

questions.question: What does the Montgomery ladder change compared to plain double-and-add (at the algorithm structure level)?
options: It performs one add and one double per scalar bit, aiming for a fixed operation pattern
It replaces all multiplications with additions, making field inversions unnecessary
It removes the need for point addition by using only x-coordinates on any curve
It guarantees the result is always in the prime-order subgroup even if the input is not
questions.explanation: The ladder structure does the same two high-level operations per bit (add+double), with selection logic based on the bit. This supports constant-time designs in low-level implementations.
